 Runoff in SW Georgia becomes high-stakes battle after House Democrats claim narrow majority
 Georgia Legislature 
 Ross Williams 
 | 
 Georgia Recorder 
 November 20th, 2026
 Stickers are seen at the Southwest Arts Center voting site on the first day for early voting in Georgia, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Atlanta. (AP Photo/Mike Stewart) 
 Voters in eight southwest Georgia counties have one more trip to make to their polling places before they ring in the new year, and they’ll decide whether House Democrats expand their newly won majority or whether Republicans can save an incumbent lawmaker’s seat.
 Early voting starts Monday for residents of Georgia’s House District 151, which includes parts of Chattahoochee, Dougherty, Marion, Schley, Stewart, Sumter, Terrell and Ware counties. Voters will choose between Republican state Rep. Mike Cheokas and Democrat Ethan Wolfe, a retired military officer, after neither candidate surpassed 50% of the vote earlier this month. Election Day is Dec. 1.
 Cheokas had the lead with 9,403 votes, good for about 47.9% to Wolfe’s 8,022 votes, or slightly under 41%. Independent candidate Travis Lockhart made up the difference.
 Democrats claimed historic wins in this year’s election, flipping every statewide position on the ballot from governor to agriculture commissioner and gaining a majority in the state House, but only a slim one.
 Democrats are set to hold 91 seats in the 180-member chamber, giving them the minimum number of seats required to claim majority status. With two other races still unresolved, Democrats expect to pick up at least one more seat when the dust settles.
 Why every vote counts
 “Anytime you get into margins that close, one vote can be the difference maker,” said Carmen Bergman, director of the Georgia House Republican Caucus. “We saw that with several pieces of consequential legislation over the years, whether it be tort reform or school choice legislation. So I expect both the Democrats and us are going to be fighting hard.”
 Both of the bills Bergman referred to passed the House with 91 votes, the minimum needed to move out of the chamber.
 “These legislators are still human,” said Democratic strategist Andrew Heaton. “People are going to get sick. People are going to have family emergencies. People are going to have deaths in the family. And so we’ve got to have every bit of cushion possible to ensure that all of our agenda goes through when it’s up for a vote.”
 Two candidates, two pitches
 Cheokas said he’s been knocking on constituents’ doors until sundown ahead of the runoff and speaking directly with voters to stress the importance of turning out.
 Cheokas, who chairs the House’s small business development committee, said his experience makes him the better man for the job.
 “Most of all, it’s about the lives of the people living in my district,” he said. “No matter who has the gavel, our community is best suited to have a representative who’s been there, knows how it works, and has a track record of delivering results. Southwest Georgians don’t want a freshman who takes orders from DC Democrats.”
 Cheokas was first sworn into the House in 2004 as a Democrat, but switched parties in 2010. He lost his seat to a Democrat in 2016 but won it back against a different opponent in 2018.
 “As for the makeup of the House, whether it’s a gubernatorial appointment, a federal indictment or a couple of sick days, we’ve seen Democrats in the House lose members during session,” he added. “That threshold for a majority will be smaller after my victory.”
 Wolfe said he and his team have been hitting the campaign trail as well and working to remind voters that the election is not over.
 He said he is pitching himself as an outsider candidate.
 “We don’t need another 20 years of the same excuses,” he said. “We need someone who shows up with fresh ideas, real solutions and a willingness to fight for the people back home. I’m talking about bringing good-paying jobs to rural Georgia, keeping our hospitals open, investing in our public schools and making life more affordable for working families.
 “I spent 30 years serving my country in the Air Force, and I know that leadership means taking responsibility and getting results,” he added. “I’m not running to build a political career. I’m running because I love this community, and I believe our best days can still be ahead of us. But we have to be willing to do something different.”
 The last time Cheokas had a Democratic challenger was in 2022, and Cheokas won by nearly 10 percentage points that year, though the area, like most of the rest of the state, swung hard toward Democrats this year. House Democrats were able to pick up 10 seats, potentially more, this year.
 That makes Heaton feel optimistic about Wolfe’s chances.
 “The reasons that animated voters to go out in November haven’t changed in one month,” he said.
 A turnout game over Thanksgiving week
 But what will change is the season. Early voting is set to last Nov. 23 to 25, the Monday through Wednesday of Thanksgiving week, when many voters will be traveling or getting ready to host family and friends and likely not thinking about who ought to represent them in the Georgia House of Representatives.
 “It’s going to take a massive field and campaign operation to get our voters back out to the polls and help them understand why this is still so important,” Heaton said. “We can’t rest where we’re at. We’ve got to get this 93rd vote.”
 Bergman said Republicans won’t be resting either and said it will come down to a “turnout game.”
 And this time around, Bergman said, Republicans will be hungry for a victory.
 “One of the best ways to know the mood of an electorate is through verbatims, what you’re hearing on the ground, what you’re hearing from people who can actually vote,” she said. “And, conservatives, Republicans in that area are motivated by what we’ve seen transpire and are excited for the chance to support their hometown guy, Mike Cheokas, to go be a watchdog in Atlanta.”
